title: CompilerDream: Learning a Compiler World Model for General Code Optimization

problem.claim: Effective code optimization depends primarily on selecting and ordering optimization passes.

gap.claim: Existing approaches either use impractically slow search algorithms or struggle to generalize to code unseen during training.

contributions.claim: CompilerDream introduces a compiler world model with reward smoothing to simulate optimization processes.
The world model supports code optimization agents based on value prediction or direct optimization-sequence generation.
The agents are trained on a large-scale program dataset for optimization across diverse application scenarios and source-code languages.

author_reported_evidence.claim: CompilerDream leads the CompilerGym leaderboard for autotuning.

The authors report that the large-scale trained compiler world model and agent outperform LLVM's built-in optimizations and state-of-the-art methods across diverse datasets in both value-prediction and end-to-end code-optimization settings.

narrative_sequence.summary: Code optimization is important, and pass selection and ordering are central to optimization success.
Fixed compiler sequences and existing search or learning approaches do not adequately provide efficient, generalizable optimization.
CompilerDream addresses the gap with a compiler world model using reward smoothing and supports agents for value prediction or direct sequence generation.
Agents trained on large-scale program data target diverse applications and source-code languages.
The authors report strong autotuning results and broad zero-shot gains over LLVM and state-of-the-art methods.

source_observation.claim: A learned world model is used to simulate optimization processes and support subsequent agent decisions.

interpretation.claim: Separating process simulation from decision generation may support multiple optimization strategies.

application.claim: For sequential optimization problems, consider learning a reusable environment model before constructing task-specific decision agents.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when world-model-based optimization is preferable to other approaches or how its costs compare.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the reward-smoothing algorithm or world-model architecture.
The abstract does not provide quantitative results, dataset details, or experimental conditions.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported performance.
